questions.corrige_markdown:
Use the sum-to-product formulae $\sin A + \sin B = 2\sin\dfrac{A+B}{2}\cos\dfrac{A-B}{2}$ and $\cos A + \cos B = 2\cos\dfrac{A+B}{2}\cos\dfrac{A-B}{2}$ with $A = 3\theta$, $B = \theta$, so that $\dfrac{A+B}{2} = 2\theta$ and $\dfrac{A-B}{2} = \theta$:

$$\sin 3\theta + \sin\theta = 2\sin 2\theta\cos\theta, \qquad \cos 3\theta + \cos\theta = 2\cos 2\theta\cos\theta.$$

Therefore, for values of $\theta$ with $\cos\theta \neq 0$ and $\cos 2\theta \neq 0$ (where both sides are defined),

$$\frac{\sin 3\theta + \sin\theta}{\cos 3\theta + \cos\theta} = \frac{2\sin 2\theta\cos\theta}{2\cos 2\theta\cos\theta} = \frac{\sin 2\theta}{\cos 2\theta} = \tan 2\theta. \qquad\blacksquare$$

(Alternative check without the factor formulae: $\sin 3\theta + \sin\theta = \sin(2\theta + \theta) + \sin(2\theta - \theta) = 2\sin 2\theta\cos\theta$, and $\cos 3\theta + \cos\theta = \cos(2\theta+\theta) + \cos(2\theta-\theta) = 2\cos 2\theta\cos\theta$. Numerical check at $\theta = 20^\circ$: left side $\dfrac{0.8660 + 0.3420}{0.5 + 0.9397} = 0.8391$ and $\tan 40^\circ = 0.8391$.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given that $f(x) = \cos x + \sqrt{3}\sin x$,

(a) Express $f(x)$ in the form $R\cos(x - \lambda)$, where $R > 0$ and $0 < \lambda < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Hence, find

(b) the minimum value of $\dfrac{1}{1 + |f(x)|}$,

(c) the general solution of $f(x) = \sqrt{3}$. (8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a)** Expand $R\cos(x - \lambda) = R\cos\lambda\cos x + R\sin\lambda\sin x$ and compare with $\cos x + \sqrt3\sin x$:

$$R\cos\lambda = 1, \qquad R\sin\lambda = \sqrt3.$$

Squaring and adding: $R^2 = 1 + 3 = 4$, so $R = 2$ (since $R > 0$). Dividing: $\tan\lambda = \sqrt3$, and $\lambda$ is in the first quadrant (both $\cos\lambda$ and $\sin\lambda$ positive) with $0 < \lambda < \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

$$\boxed{f(x) = 2\cos\!\left(x - \frac{\pi}{3}\right)}$$

Check: $2\cos(x - \pi/3) = 2\left(\tfrac12\cos x + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin x\right) = \cos x + \sqrt3\sin x$.

**(b)** Since $-1 \le \cos(x - \pi/3) \le 1$, we have $0 \le |f(x)| \le 2$. The fraction $\dfrac{1}{1 + |f(x)|}$ decreases as $|f(x)|$ increases, so it is smallest when $|f(x)|$ is largest, i.e. $|f(x)| = 2$:

$$\boxed{\text{minimum value} = \frac{1}{1 + 2} = \frac13}$$

It is reached when $\cos(x - \pi/3) = \pm 1$, i.e. $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + n\pi$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. (The largest value of the fraction is $1$, when $f(x) = 0$.)

**(c)** Solve $2\cos(x - \pi/3) = \sqrt3$, i.e. $\cos(x - \pi/3) = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. The principal value is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and $\cos\alpha = \cos\beta$ gives $\alpha = \pm\beta + 2n\pi$:

$$x - \frac{\pi}{3} = \pm\frac{\pi}{6} + 2n\pi, \quad n \in \mathbb{Z}.$$

- with $+$: $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{\pi}{6} + 2n\pi = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi$;
- with $-$: $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{6} + 2n\pi = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + 2n\pi$.

$$\boxed{x = \frac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi \quad\text{or}\quad x = \frac{\pi}{6} + 2n\pi, \qquad n \in \mathbb{Z}}$$

Check: $f(\pi/2) = 0 + \sqrt3 = \sqrt3$ and $f(\pi/6) = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} + \sqrt3\cdot\tfrac12 = \sqrt3$.
